661: B is correct because Amazon RDS Proxy is a fully managed, highly available database proxy that pools and shares connections to the RDS database, so applications can handle far more simultaneous connections during weekend and seasonal peaks without exhausting the database. The applications only need to be pointed at the RDS Proxy endpoint, and AWS operates the proxy infrastructure, giving the least operational overhead. A custom EC2 proxy or Lambda-based pooling would require the company to build, patch, and run that infrastructure itself.
662: D is correct because deleting nonessential snapshots immediately removes accumulated snapshot storage costs, and Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates snapshot creation, retention, and deletion according to the company's policy, so costs stay optimized without ongoing manual effort. Simply deleting all expired snapshots once does not prevent costs from growing again, and reducing volume size does not address snapshot costs at all.
663: A is correct because a single customer managed AWS KMS key can encrypt both the S3 bucket and the RDS for MySQL database, and its key policy can grant encrypt and decrypt permissions only to the ECS task execution role. Since the encrypted data cannot be read without those KMS operations, only the ECS cluster's tasks can access the sensitive data in both services. AWS managed keys do not allow the customer to customize the key policy to restrict access this way.
664: A is correct because burstable performance instances in unlimited mode can sustain the sudden 10x spike in CPU utilization by drawing surplus credits instead of being throttled, keeping the application responsive during the twice-monthly events. Configuring the Elastic Beanstalk environment to scale based on requests automatically adds instances when demand increases, improving latency at peak hours. Scheduled or predictive scaling patterns do not fit unpredictable twice-monthly spikes well.
665: B is correct because AWS CloudFormation lets the company provision its systems and network infrastructure automatically through code, and AWS Config continuously records configuration changes to resources so the security team can track and audit every incremental change. This pairing directly satisfies both the automation and audit requirements. Service Catalog governs approved product portfolios rather than tracking infrastructure changes, and Organizations consolidates accounts but does not deploy infrastructure.
666: B is correct because migrating to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance creates a synchronous standby replica in another Availability Zone with automatic failover, giving the MySQL database high availability without any application changes. E is correct because the application is stateless, so an Application Load Balancer distributing traffic to an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances across two Availability Zones removes the single-instance point of failure and automatically replaces unhealthy instances. Together these actions achieve high availability while leaving the application code untouched.
667: C is correct because an interface endpoint for Amazon S3, powered by AWS PrivateLink, keeps all S3 traffic on the private AWS network and is reachable both from resources in the Region and from the on-premises network over the existing Direct Connect connection, so the data never traverses the internet. Gateway endpoints can only be accessed from within the VPC and cannot be reached from on-premises, which is why they do not fit.
668: D is correct because a tag policy in AWS Organizations can define a list of allowed values for the application name tag and enforce that tagging compliance across all accounts in the organization, preventing tagging operations that use noncompliant values so resources can only be created with approved application names. IAM groups and resource groups cannot validate and enforce allowed tag values at resource creation time across multiple accounts.
669: C is correct because AWS Secrets Manager natively integrates with Amazon RDS to provide built-in, automated rotation of the master user password on a schedule the company defines, such as every 30 days, with the rotation handled entirely by the service. This eliminates the custom code, scheduling, and manual password changes required by the other options, making it the least operational overhead choice.
670: B is correct because the workload is predictable: it runs only 4 hours once a week and the company knows the exact number of read and write operations per second, so provisioned mode with appropriately configured RCUs and WCUs costs far less than on-demand pricing. Reserved capacity only makes sense for steady, continuous usage and would be wasted on a table that is used 4 hours per week.
671: B is correct because AWS Cost Anomaly Detection applies machine learning to the company's historical cost data to detect unusual spending patterns and can automatically notify responsible stakeholders, for example through Amazon SNS alerts, when anomalous spend is identified. This directly satisfies both the monitoring and notification requirements. Budgets and the Pricing Calculator track planned or known costs rather than detecting unusual spending.
672: B is correct because an AWS Glue crawler automatically scans the clickstream data in Amazon S3, infers the schema, and populates the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and Amazon Athena then provides serverless, standard SQL querying of that data directly in S3. This serverless pipeline requires no clusters or infrastructure to manage, giving the least operational overhead for quick analysis before deciding on further processing.
673: B is correct because an Amazon S3 File Gateway presents an SMB interface backed by S3, so files frequently accessed during the first 7 days are served from cache with low latency, and an S3 Lifecycle policy automatically transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days. Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class, and its standard retrieval completes within 12 hours, meeting the maximum 24-hour retrieval requirement.
674: B is correct because creating a read replica for the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance offloads the heavy read traffic from the primary instance, allowing reads to scale independently of writes and improving application performance during high traffic. D is correct because an Amazon ElastiCache cluster caches common query results in memory, dramatically reducing the number of read queries that reach the database and further cutting latency. A Multi-AZ standby instance cannot serve read traffic, so it does not help with the read load.
675: D is correct because EBS snapshot lock prevents the locked snapshots from being deleted, guarding against accidental deletion, and it enforces this protection as a property of the snapshots themselves rather than through IAM, so the storage administrator's permissions remain unchanged. Because no policies or roles need to be created and maintained, this requires the least administrative effort. An IAM deny policy would alter the administrator's rights, which the requirements forbid.
676: B is correct because VPC Flow Logs capture information about traffic to and from the network interfaces in near real time and can publish it to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, and Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose can continuously stream those logs directly into an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain for analysis. Kinesis Data Streams would require an additional consumer application to read and load the data, and CloudTrail records API events rather than network traffic.
677: B is correct because two managed node groups, one provisioned with On-Demand Instances for a reliable baseline and one with Spot Instances for cost savings, provide the most cost-effective configuration for a development cluster that is used infrequently. Managed node groups also mean EKS provisions and manages the lifecycle of all the nodes, meeting the requirement that the cluster manage the nodes. A self-managed Auto Scaling group would leave node management to the company, and a single all-Spot or all-On-Demand group is either less resilient or more expensive.
678: B is correct because a customer managed AWS KMS key gives the company full control over the key lifecycle, including the ability to create, rotate on demand, and disable the key, and SSE-KMS uses that key for server-side encryption of the S3 objects with minimal effort. AWS managed keys cannot be rotated or disabled on customer demand, and SSE-S3 offers no customer control over the encryption keys.
679: A is correct because creating the S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled, which requires versioning, provides write-once-read-many retention that protects the backup objects from being altered or removed during the retention period. C is correct because configuring a default retention period of 30 days automatically applies that retention to every object placed in the bucket, ensuring the backups are retained for the required 30 days. E is correct because an S3 Lifecycle policy that expires objects after 30 days automatically deletes them once the retention window ends, meeting the automatic-deletion requirement.
680: A is correct because AWS DataSync supports S3 buckets and EFS file systems as locations, tasks can be scheduled to run continuously as new files arrive in the source bucket, and the transfer mode that moves only changed data ensures files are copied or overwritten only when the source file actually changes. This is a fully managed service, so it meets the continuous-copy requirement with the least operational overhead, whereas custom scripts, EC2 instances, or Lambda functions all require the company to build and maintain code.
